content:
After a week of fierce competition, Backpack emerged victorious to claim the "Fat Bear Week" crown, becoming the most robust bear in Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.

The nonprofit organisation that hosts this long-running contest announced the results on Tuesday, saying the bear, known for its docile nature, received over 100,000 votes, narrowly defeating Bear 910 with just over 50 percent of the votes.

Now in its twelfth year, the contest aims to celebrate the resilient spirit of the 2,200 brown bears residing in the Alaska Peninsula Preserve, which stretches from the southwestern tip of the state toward the Aleutian Islands. Fat Bear Week was founded in 2014 as an interactive way to introduce the public to brown bears—the coastal cousins of grizzlies.

Last year's champion, "Chunk" (officially designated Bear 32), won the previous year weighing in at approximately 1,200 pounds. This year he was defeated in the first round by Bucky, who then went on to lose to Backpack (officially Bear 89) in subsequent matchups.

A total of sixteen bears competed for this year's "fattest" honours in a single-elimination format. Voting took place on the fatbearweek.org website, with the winner announced after the final round of voting closed on Tuesday evening. Members of the public can observe the bears via live cameras on explore.org and then cast their votes for their favourites.

"Fat bears are successful bears," the organisation wrote on its website. These bears return to the salmon-rich waters of Brooks River in late June to feast, packing on fat to prepare for winter. To qualify for the contest, bears must frequent the river area.

Backpack is the offspring of former Fat Bear Week champion Holly, who brought him to Brooks River in 2006 when he was still a first-year cub. His name comes from his habit of climbing onto his mother's back when crossing the river. This year's supporters rallied behind him in comments on the contest's Instagram page, citing his bloodline and his reputation as a "gentle giant."

Backpack's contest profile read: "Unlike many large adult male brown bears, Backpack rarely displays aggression toward competitors."

Rather than winning through fighting, Backpack triumphed through what could be described as a quiet strength, with wildlife cameras frequently capturing him sitting on a rock downstream as if admiring the scenery around him.

The Bear 910 he defeated is also a daughter of former champion "409 Beadnose."

Adult male brown bears typically weigh between 600 and 900 pounds (approximately 270 to 410 kilograms) in midsummer. After gorging on salmon returning to spawn and preparing for hibernation, larger males can weigh over 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). Females tend to weigh roughly one-third less. At this time of year, bears may consume up to 30 fish per day, seeking to pack a full year's worth of sustenance into roughly six months.

During winter hibernation, bears neither eat nor drink, and can lose up to one-third of their body weight.

Fat Bear Week contestants also include five bear families, recognising this summer's record-breaking numbers of bear families and cubs at Brooks River. Bear mothers must take in enough calories to sustain themselves through hibernation while also feeding and protecting their cubs. Cubs commonly face the risk of attacks by other bears amid territorial disputes and food scarcity.

Bear 132 advanced to the semifinals with her three spring cubs, but was defeated by Bear 910.

According to her contest profile, Bear 132 is already one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River. In July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days, wandering alone around the river channel before being reunited days later.

___

AP writer Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.
